case-sara.text: [Softly] Shouldn't I just focus on positive thoughts instead of digging into how sad I am?
case-sara.suggestion: You want some relief from the sadness. Positive thoughts may help, and we can also listen to what you are grieving and needing. We can take it slowly, without spending the whole session in the pain.

case-sara.text: [Embarrassed] Why keep asking what I feel when I just need a plan for getting through the week?
case-sara.suggestion: We can make a plan for the week. Listening to what is hardest can help us choose what belongs in it: perhaps company, rest, or help with a difficult evening. The feelings help us make the plan fit you.

case-sara.text: [Tearful] I feel embarrassed crying about this again. How does making room for tears help me move on?
case-sara.suggestion: The tears may help us notice what still hurts and what you need as you adjust to the loss. Crying is not a task you have to complete. We can make room for the sadness and pause when you need to.

case-sara.text: [Embarrassed] If distraction gets me through the quiet hours, why would we mess with that?
case-sara.suggestion: Distraction helps you get through those hours, and we can keep what works. We can also explore a little of what makes the quiet hard, so we understand what support you need when distraction is not enough.

case-sara.text: [Worried] How does talking about a breakup help when other people have bigger problems?
case-sara.suggestion: This breakup is affecting your life, even if others have different problems. Exploring what hurts can help us understand what you need to get through it. You do not have to prove the pain is big enough to deserve attention.

case-sara.text: [Tearful] If we talk about him more, won't that keep him in my head even longer?
case-sara.suggestion: You are worried that talking will keep you stuck on him. The aim is to understand what comes up for you when you miss him, rather than go over every detail about him. That can help us find what you need now.

case-sara.text: [Hesitant] Can we set goals so I am busy enough not to feel this?
case-sara.suggestion: We can set goals that give the day some structure. I also want to understand what happens when the sadness returns. That can help us choose activities and support that matter to you, rather than rely on staying busy every moment.

case-sara.text: [Worried] What if 'hollow' is all I have? I don't know how to make that useful.
case-sara.suggestion: We can begin with "hollow"; you do not need a better word. Exploring when that emptiness comes and what it is like may help us understand what you are missing. We do not have to turn it into a different feeling.

case-sara.text: [Impatient] I want a timeline for when I stop checking his profile; otherwise this feels pointless.
case-sara.suggestion: You want to know when this will change. I cannot give you a date, but we can look at what you hope to find when you check and how you feel afterwards. Understanding that pattern may help us find other ways to meet the need.

case-sara.text: [Worried] How is this different from retelling the breakup until even I am sick of hearing it?
case-sara.suggestion: You do not want to keep repeating the same story. We can pause at a moment that still hurts and explore what it means to you now. The aim is to understand what you need, not to go through every detail of the breakup again.

case-sara.text: [Unsure] Some weeks I cry more in here, and some weeks I don't. How will we know this is helping, apart from how emotional I get?
case-sara.suggestion: You want a way to recognise change beyond tears. In this work we look at whether you can understand what you feel and need, and respond to yourself with less blame. We can agree on signs that matter to you and review them together; being more emotional isn't the goal.

case-sara.text: [Curious] If I know the breakup is why I'm upset, what else are we trying to find out by staying with the feeling?
case-sara.suggestion: Knowing the cause matters. Staying with the feeling can help distinguish the sadness of losing him from the blame you turn on yourself, so we can respond to each more helpfully. We can try this with one small moment, if you want.

case-michael.text: [Skeptical] I came for anger control, not feelings talk. How does this stop me from blowing up?
case-michael.suggestion: You want to stop the outbursts. We can slow down what happens just before your voice rises and notice the feelings involved. Recognizing that moment may give you more room to choose how you respond.

case-michael.text: [Defensive] Isn't looking for the trigger just making excuses for me blowing up?
case-michael.suggestion: Understanding what sets off the anger does not remove your responsibility for what you do. It can help us notice the reaction sooner and work on a different response. The aim is to change the behavior, not explain it away.

case-michael.text: [Tense] Why slow down when people are watching and I need to look in control?
case-michael.suggestion: You want to look in control when people are watching. A short pause can give you time to notice what has hit you before you answer. We can practice a pause that helps you respond firmly without raising your voice.

case-michael.text: [Worried] How does going near shame help if my wife or team see that as weakness?
case-michael.suggestion: You worry that showing shame will cost you respect. Exploring it here can help you understand what happens when you feel exposed. You do not have to reveal it to your wife or team in order to work on how you respond.

case-michael.text: [Challenging] Can we skip the feelings and just build a tool for when my chest gets hot?
case-michael.suggestion: We can work on something you can use when your chest gets hot. Understanding what you feel at that moment helps us choose a useful response: perhaps pausing, setting a limit, or saying what bothered you. We do not have to start with a long explanation.

case-michael.text: [Worried] How does noticing a tight jaw help me lead when a meeting turns tense?
case-michael.suggestion: You want to handle a tense meeting well. Your jaw tightening can be a cue to pause and notice what is happening before you answer. The point is to understand your reaction early enough to choose a response that fits the situation.

case-michael.text: [Worried] What if I blow up after all this and everyone says therapy failed?
case-michael.suggestion: Another outburst would matter, and we would need to take its effect seriously. It would also give us something specific to review: what happened before it, what you noticed, and where a different response was possible. That helps us decide what to work on next.

case-michael.text: [Worried] How does more talking prove to my wife that I can stop exploding?
case-michael.suggestion: Your wife will need to see changes in what you do. Exploring the anger can help us understand how it builds and practice a different response. We can then look honestly at whether there are fewer outbursts and whether you take responsibility when one happens.

case-michael.text: [Challenging] Will this change how my team sees me, or just make me analyze myself?
case-michael.suggestion: You want the work to make a difference in how you lead. Understanding what happens when you feel challenged can help us practice a different tone or response. We can judge its usefulness by what changes with the team, not by how much you can analyze.

case-michael.text: [Embarrassed] What am I supposed to do if I am not good at feelings and have no words?
case-michael.suggestion: You do not need to be good at describing feelings to start. We can use something you already notice, like heat or a tight jaw, and explore what happens around it. Those clues can help us understand the reaction before you have a name for it.

case-michael.text: [Sceptical] I need to stop snapping. How does telling you I felt embarrassed in a meeting help me do that at home?
case-michael.suggestion: You want a change you can use at home. Noticing the embarrassment before it becomes anger may help you catch the reaction earlier and choose how to respond, rather than only fighting the anger afterwards. We can begin with a manageable moment you choose.

case-michael.text: [Practical] Couldn't we agree on a rule for arguments? If I have a rule, I can follow it. Feelings don't seem very reliable.
case-michael.suggestion: A rule can be useful. We're also looking at what happens when criticism hits, because understanding that reaction can make it easier to use the rule when you most need it. We can keep it practical and check what is useful to you.

case-jason.text: [Skeptical] Does this actually help social anxiety, or am I just learning to stare at fear?
case-jason.suggestion: You want to know how this helps outside the room. We can explore what feels threatening when people look at you, and practice staying with a manageable amount of that feeling. The aim is to make speaking less of a battle with yourself.

case-jason.text: [Blank] What if I go blank here too and waste the whole session?
case-jason.suggestion: Going blank would be something for us to understand, not a failure of the session. We can slow down and notice what happens when the words go. That may help us find a way to support you without adding pressure to speak.

case-jason.text: [Anxious] My thoughts are what ruin things, so why keep asking about my chest?
case-jason.suggestion: The thoughts matter. I ask about your chest because physical sensations can give us another clue to what you are experiencing. We can explore both, and see which helps you recognize the anxiety and what you need in that moment.

case-jason.text: [Worried] When I pay attention to fear it gets louder, so why would I practice that?
case-jason.suggestion: You notice that focusing on fear makes it stronger. We need to take that seriously and adjust the pace. The aim is to understand a manageable part of your experience, with room to pause, rather than make you endure more fear.

case-jason.text: [Hesitant] Can we just script what I should say before meetings so I do not freeze?
case-jason.suggestion: We can prepare a sentence for meetings. I also want to understand what happens when you freeze, because having words ready may not be enough then. We can practice the sentence alongside noticing what helps you stay present.

case-jason.text: [Anxious] How long before I can speak in meetings without my body taking over?
case-jason.suggestion: I cannot promise a timetable. We can work on recognizing what happens when attention turns to you, and look together for changes such as staying present a little longer or recovering more easily afterwards. Those changes matter even before the anxiety is gone.

case-jason.text: [Embarrassed] I'm embarrassed to talk about being this scared; how is saying it out loud supposed to help?
case-jason.suggestion: Saying it aloud can help us understand the fear together instead of leaving you to handle it alone. You can share a little and see how it feels to be heard. We do not have to force it if the embarrassment becomes too much.

case-jason.text: [Worried] What do I actually do when the 'you're awkward' voice starts?
case-jason.suggestion: We can notice what that voice says and how it affects you, then practice a response that feels believable. The aim is to give you something to turn to when the criticism starts, without having to win an argument with it.

case-jason.text: [Hesitant] Will I always have to work this hard just to speak like everyone else?
case-jason.suggestion: You want speaking to take less effort. I cannot promise how quickly that will happen. We can work with the fear and self-criticism, and look for changes such as saying a little more or recovering more easily after a difficult conversation.

case-jason.text: [Quietly] Why practice eye contact when it feels like people can see everything wrong with me?
case-jason.suggestion: Eye contact is not a requirement. If being seen is something you want to work on, we can explore what makes it feel exposing and choose a small step together. The aim is more freedom to connect, not a particular way of looking at people.

case-jason.text: [Worried] When you ask me to notice a feeling, I start checking whether I'm doing it correctly. Isn't that more of the same problem?
case-jason.suggestion: That checking is important information, not a failed exercise. We can notice the pressure itself, without requiring a particular feeling, and practise a less judging way of paying attention.

case-jason.text: [Hesitant] I can talk about a meeting afterwards. But when I'm actually there, my mind goes blank. What are we practising here that could help there?
case-jason.suggestion: You want this to reach those difficult moments. Here we can slowly notice what happens just before the blankness, so you have more chance of recognising it without immediately judging yourself. You can choose where we start.

case-laura.text: [Worried] If this is my brain chemistry, why would talking to you change anything?
case-laura.suggestion: You are wondering whether talking can help if there is a biological part to this. We do not have to choose just one explanation. Here we can explore your experience and what helps you feel more present and connected, alongside any medical care.

case-laura.text: [Slow and flat] How do I know this will not make me relive trauma when I already disappear?
case-laura.suggestion: You already know how easily you can feel far away. We can begin with what you notice now, without asking you to relive the trauma. Small steps and pauses help us find a pace you can stay with, and we can adjust if it becomes too much.

case-laura.text: [Slow and flat] If I go numb before I can feel anything, what exactly are we working with?
case-laura.suggestion: The numbness is something we can explore without deciding why it is there. We can notice when it changes, what comes just before it, and what helps you stay present. That gives us a place to begin without forcing a feeling.

case-laura.text: [Worried] What if your kindness makes me more suspicious instead of safer?
case-laura.suggestion: Then the suspicion belongs in our conversation too. Understanding what feels hard to trust can help us decide how to work together. You do not have to feel safer just because I am kind, or trust more quickly than you do.

case-laura.text: [Hesitant] Will this dig up things I cannot handle and leave me worse afterward?
case-laura.suggestion: You are worried about how you will feel afterwards. We can agree on what to leave aside, begin with a small amount, and check how you are before the session ends. How you feel afterwards also matters; it helps us adjust the work rather than push ahead.

case-laura.text: [Slow and flat] Why chase tiny signals if I shut down before I can use them?
case-laura.suggestion: You worry that you will shut down before any of this helps. Small signs can help us notice when the work is becoming too much, so we can slow down or pause sooner. We are trying to work at a pace you can stay with.

case-laura.text: [Slow and flat] How is talking supposed to change this flatness when I barely feel anything?
case-laura.suggestion: We can begin with the flatness itself: what it is like, when it changes, and how it affects your days. The aim is to understand your experience and find what helps you feel more connected. You do not have to produce a strong feeling for the work to count.

case-laura.text: [Slow and flat] How will I know this is working if I still feel numb most days?
case-laura.suggestion: We can look for changes that matter to you, even if numbness is still there: a moment of interest, less strain with someone close, or being able to stay present a little longer. Checking those changes together helps us decide whether the work is useful.

case-laura.text: [Hesitant] Can we just talk about practical things so I do not have to feel all this?
case-laura.suggestion: We can talk about practical things. I would also like to understand what makes the feelings hard to approach, so any plan takes that into account. We can begin with everyday life without asking you to go into painful memories.

case-laura.text: [Worried] What if I freeze in here and you sit there waiting for an answer?
case-laura.suggestion: If you freeze, I do not want to add pressure by waiting for an answer. We can pause and find what helps you notice the room or my voice. Understanding those moments is part of finding a way to work together that you can stay present for.

case-laura.text: [Flat] I spend my working day helping people cope. I don't understand why talking about what hurts is better than learning to cope with it.
case-laura.suggestion: Coping matters, and we won't take it away. We can also approach a little of what the numbness keeps at a distance, so coping doesn't have to mean being cut off from everything you feel. You can choose how much we approach.

case-laura.text: [Guarded] You say we don't have to discuss the past. Then how can this work if the past is what's wrong with me?
case-laura.suggestion: We don't have to retell painful events to begin. We can work with how closeness or numbness feels here, in small amounts you choose, and learn what helps you stay present now.

case-carlos.text: [Defensive] Is this going to make me soft? I still need people to know not to mess with me.
case-carlos.suggestion: You want to be able to stand up for yourself. Understanding your feelings does not mean giving up your boundaries. It can help you speak firmly without using anger to frighten people or losing sight of what you want to say.

case-carlos.text: [Tense] Why talk feelings instead of giving me tools I can use when I am heated?
case-carlos.suggestion: We can work on something you can use when the anger rises. Understanding what you feel just before it helps us choose what to practice, such as stepping away or saying what bothered you. The point is to turn that understanding into a different action.

case-carlos.text: [Tense and angry] How does this help when someone disrespects me in front of my family?
case-carlos.suggestion: You want to respond when someone disrespects you. Exploring what happens inside can help us separate what you want to say from the urge to lash out. Then we can practice a firm response that does not frighten or hurt anyone.

case-carlos.text: [Skeptical] How does feeling more keep me from losing my edge and getting walked over?
case-carlos.suggestion: You worry that understanding your feelings means giving up your strength. The aim is to help you recognize what matters and set a clear limit, while taking responsibility for how you treat people. We can work on being firm without using intimidation.

case-carlos.text: [Defensive] If anger is what protects me, why would I spend therapy trying to feel what is underneath it?
case-carlos.suggestion: Anger feels protective, and you want to keep that protection. Exploring what sets it off can help us understand what you need to stand up for. We can work on protecting your boundaries without letting the anger become harmful.

case-carlos.text: [Tense] How is breathing supposed to matter when I'm already two seconds from snapping?
case-carlos.suggestion: When you are that close to snapping, breathing alone may not be enough. We also need to understand how the pressure builds before that point. Noticing the earlier signs can help you step away before anyone is frightened or hurt.

case-carlos.text: [Tense and angry] How do I demand respect without acting like somebody can walk over me?
case-carlos.suggestion: We can work on saying clearly what you will and will not accept. Understanding the feeling behind that need for respect helps us choose words for it. The goal is a boundary you can stand by without making a threat.

case-carlos.text: [Defensive] I learned you have to hit first, so why would slowing down help?
case-carlos.suggestion: You learned to hit first when you expected danger. We need ways to respond now that do not harm people. Slowing down lets us examine what feels threatening and practice another action, such as stepping away before you strike.

case-carlos.text: [Guilty] My kid saw me angry. How does talking about feelings help him?
case-carlos.suggestion: Talking alone cannot undo what your child saw. Understanding how the anger builds can help you work on changing what happens at home. That also includes taking responsibility with your child, without asking them to make you feel better about it.

case-carlos.text: [Defensive] How do we keep this from becoming years of talk while my family waits?
case-carlos.suggestion: You want your family to see change soon. We can focus on the situations where the anger does most harm, understand what happens before it, and practice another response. We also need to check what actually changes at home, rather than assume that talking is enough.

case-carlos.text: [Sceptical] When you ask what the anger feels like, I think you're asking me to get more worked up. That's exactly what I'm trying to stop.
case-carlos.suggestion: You want to avoid getting carried away. We can approach the anger in small amounts and notice what sets it off, without acting on it, so you have more choice before it takes over.

case-carlos.text: [Firm] I don't want to spend an hour feeling sorry for myself. I want my family to stop being afraid of me.
case-carlos.suggestion: Your family's safety is the goal. Understanding the hurt or threat around your anger can help you recognise it sooner and respond without intimidation; it doesn't excuse frightening them. We can approach it without pushing you past what you can manage.

case-nina.text: [Guilty] Isn't it selfish to focus on my feelings when everyone needs something from me?
case-nina.suggestion: It feels selfish to turn toward your own feelings. They can help us notice your needs and limits, including when you are exhausted. Making room for those needs is part of finding ways to care for others without wearing yourself out.

case-nina.text: [Apologetic] What does noticing my body even do when guilt hits before I think?
case-nina.suggestion: Noticing your body gives us another way to recognize the guilt, even when it comes before a clear thought. That can help us pause and understand what you need before deciding whether to say yes. We can begin with whatever you already notice.

case-nina.text: [Worried] How is emotion work supposed to help when I need practical steps before I drown?
case-nina.suggestion: You need something to change in daily life. Listening to your feelings can help us understand where the load is too much and what support or limit you need. We can use that to choose one practical step, rather than give you another list to manage.

case-nina.text: [Worried] How does focusing on guilt help me say no when I already feel bad?
case-nina.suggestion: The aim is not to make you feel more guilty. We can explore what saying no seems to mean about you, and whether the guilt fits what you are actually asking for. That helps us work on a limit you can stand by, even if guilt is still there.

case-nina.text: [Worried] If people might leave when I stop helping, how is naming needs supposed to help?
case-nina.suggestion: Naming your needs cannot guarantee that someone will stay. It helps us understand what you want from the relationship, what you fear, and who is able to respond. We can consider those things together before you decide what to ask for.

case-nina.text: [Hesitant] Can we just fix my schedule? Talking about needs sounds like another task.
case-nina.suggestion: You want less to do, not another assignment. We can look at the schedule together. Paying attention to your needs helps us decide what actually has to change, rather than make you better at fitting everything in.

case-nina.text: [Worried] What if saying no always feels wrong no matter how much we talk?
case-nina.suggestion: You do not have to wait for saying no to feel easy. We can understand what brings the guilt and practice a small limit that fits your needs and responsibilities. The aim is more choice, even while the feeling is there.

case-nina.text: [Worried] How does asking for help get easier when needing anything feels like too much?
case-nina.suggestion: We can begin with a small, specific request and notice what makes it hard to ask. That helps us understand the shame and choose someone you can reasonably turn to. You do not have to ask for everything at once.

case-nina.text: [Guilty] If I focus on needs, won't I become the needy person I dislike?
case-nina.suggestion: You are afraid that having needs will change you into someone you dislike. Exploring them can help you choose what to ask for and where to set a limit, instead of waiting until you are worn out. You can value caring for others and make room for yourself.

case-nina.text: [Tired] How will I know this is actually helping and not just making me more self-focused?
case-nina.suggestion: We can look for changes you actually want: asking for help more directly, getting some rest, or saying no when you are exhausted. That helps us check whether attention to your feelings is changing daily life.

case-nina.text: [Apologetic] I could name what I need for a whole hour. Then I go home and everyone still needs things. What would actually be different?
case-nina.suggestion: Naming your needs won't remove the demands. It can help you recognise your own limits before exhaustion makes every choice harder, so caring for others can include caring for yourself. We can begin with a situation you want to understand.

case-nina.text: [Worried] If we make room for my resentment, won't I just become less kind? Being useful is something I actually value.
case-nina.suggestion: We can respect how much kindness matters to you. Listening to resentment may help you notice when giving has gone beyond what you can sustain, rather than letting it build until kindness feels impossible. We can listen to just a little of it at a time.

case-aisha.text: [Worried] What if talking about being left makes me want to hurt myself again before I can stop it?
case-aisha.suggestion: That fear needs our attention before we go into the pain. First, I need to understand whether you might hurt yourself now. Then we can agree on support and pacing; exploring feelings should not mean pushing you beyond what you can manage.

case-aisha.text: [Desperate] I need you to promise you will never leave, or I do not see how this helps.
case-aisha.suggestion: You need to know what you can rely on. I cannot promise never to leave, but I can be clear about our appointments, contact, and any ending. Exploring what those limits bring up can help us plan support for the times that feel hardest.

case-aisha.text: [Panicked] If you cancel, how does naming the alarm stop me from doing something drastic?
case-aisha.suggestion: Naming the fear alone is not enough. When you say "something drastic", do you mean hurting yourself or ending your life? We need to understand that first, then agree on what support you can use if a session is cancelled.

case-aisha.text: [Worried] What if my feelings are too much for any therapist to work with?
case-aisha.suggestion: You worry that your feelings will be too much, even here. We can begin with a small part and notice what helps or makes it harder. That helps us choose the pace and support you need, rather than ask you to bring everything at once.

case-aisha.text: [Panicked] When I am panicking, why ask about feet and breathing instead of just calming me down?
case-aisha.suggestion: I am trying to help you notice something in the room while the panic is strong. The chair or the floor may give you a point to return to. We can see whether that helps; if focusing on your breathing makes it worse, we do not need to do that.

case-aisha.text: [Desperate] How does working with this neediness help when reassurance from you feels so urgent?
case-aisha.suggestion: Reassurance feels urgent, and you want something that helps beyond this moment. We can explore what happens when you fear losing contact, and practice asking for support within clear boundaries. The aim is to find more ways to cope than reassurance from me alone.

case-aisha.text: [Panicked] If we focus on this relationship, won't I get attached and then fall apart when it ends?
case-aisha.suggestion: You are worried about becoming attached and then facing an ending. We can talk openly about the relationship and its limits from the start. Understanding what closeness and separation bring up helps us plan the work and an ending, rather than leave that fear unspoken.

case-aisha.text: [Worried] How will this help my relationships not blow up when I switch from begging to pushing away?
case-aisha.suggestion: We can explore what happens just before you shift from asking someone to stay to pushing them away. Understanding the feelings at that point helps us practice saying what you need more directly, or taking a pause before the conversation becomes a fight.

case-aisha.text: [Hesitant] Will this take forever, or am I always going to be this intense?
case-aisha.suggestion: You want to know whether things can change, and how long it will take. I cannot promise a timetable. We can look for changes that matter to you, such as getting through a goodbye with more support or recovering more easily after a difficult exchange.

case-aisha.text: [Mistrustful] Every therapist boundary sounds like distance, so why would I trust this?
case-aisha.suggestion: You hear a limit as distance, so simply asking you to trust it would miss the fear. We can explore what each boundary means to you while being clear about what I can offer. That helps us make the work more predictable without promising that the fear will vanish.

case-aisha.text: [Urgent] I can name every feeling. It doesn't stop me panicking when someone goes quiet. What is supposed to happen after I name it?
case-aisha.suggestion: Naming is only a beginning. We can work slowly with the panic and what you need in that moment, so you aren't left just describing it or urgently trying to make someone else remove it.

case-aisha.text: [Sceptical, scared] If we practise being with the fear here, does that mean you're teaching me to accept people leaving me?
case-aisha.suggestion: Your need for connection matters. The aim is to understand the fear and what you need, so panic doesn't have to decide every action. We can approach it at a pace you choose; needing people isn't something we're trying to remove.

case-david.text: [Controlled] Why focus on feelings when I need results people can actually see?
case-david.suggestion: You want changes that show in daily life. Feelings are part of what happens before you withdraw or speak sharply. Understanding those moments can help you choose how to respond, and we can check together whether it makes a difference at home and work.

case-david.text: [Skeptical] How is this practical if I do not want to be psychoanalyzed or reduced to childhood?
case-david.suggestion: We stay practical by starting with present moments you want changed. History comes in only if it helps explain why a reaction gets so fast or intense, so the work stays in service of steadier choices now.

case-david.text: [Challenging] Will this help my marriage or is this just about me?
case-david.suggestion: Your responses are part of what happens between you and your wife. Exploring what you feel before you withdraw or speak sharply can help you choose a different response. We can check whether that changes the conversations, without assuming your work alone will fix the marriage.

case-david.text: [Controlled] I already know the theory. Why spend time on feelings instead of fixing behavior?
case-david.suggestion: Knowing the theory and noticing your reaction in the moment are different things. We can look closely at what you feel just before the behavior you want to change. That gives us something specific to practice, beyond knowing how it should work.

case-david.text: [Wounded but sharp] My emotions are the problem. Why would we focus on the thing that keeps messing everything up?
case-david.suggestion: You see how much damage the reactions cause. Exploring the feelings can help us understand what happens before they turn into withdrawal or sharp words. The aim is to give you more choice about what you do with the feeling, not make it stronger.

case-david.text: [Demanding] I need anger control, not a deep dive into what I feel under it.
case-david.suggestion: You want to stop the anger doing damage. We can work on that directly, including what happens before an outburst. Looking at the feelings involved is a way to recognize the build-up earlier, not a requirement to reveal everything at once.

case-david.text: [Challenging] Can we skip childhood stuff and stay with what is happening now?
case-david.suggestion: Yes, we can stay present-focused. We only name earlier patterns if they show up in today's reactions, so history serves change instead of becoming a detour.

case-david.text: [Worried] What if I do not feel anything when you ask me to look inside?
case-david.suggestion: Not feeling anything is a place to begin, not a failed exercise. We can explore what that is like and whether you notice even a small change as we talk. The purpose is to understand your experience, without requiring a feeling you do not have.

case-david.text: [Demanding] I need quick wins; I do not want another endless insight project.
case-david.suggestion: You want something to change soon. We can choose one situation where your reaction causes problems and work on what you feel before it happens. Then we can check whether a different response helps, rather than measure progress by insight alone.

case-david.text: [Controlled] How will I know this is worth it instead of another insight project?
case-david.suggestion: We use concrete markers because insight alone will not be enough: less shutdown in hard conversations, quicker repair after you miss, and more room to stay present when shame gets hit.

case-david.text: [Coolly] I can explain my childhood perfectly well. It hasn't changed anything. Why would another conversation about feelings be different?
case-david.suggestion: You want more than another explanation. The aim is to notice what happens to you as you speak, so we can meet the hurt in the moment rather than only explain it afterwards. We can try a small piece and check how it is for you.

case-david.text: [Guarded] If I let you see how much the criticism hurt, what stops this turning into an exercise in taking me down a peg?
case-david.suggestion: Being diminished is precisely what you don't want. The aim is to understand the injury beneath the need to defend yourself, without stripping away your dignity; you can tell me when the work feels diminishing.

case-marcus.text: [Flat] Talking will not change what happened, so why open the door to it?
case-marcus.suggestion: You are right that talking cannot change what happened. The aim is to help with how it affects your life now. We can begin with what you notice today, without asking you to retell the worst parts of the past.

case-marcus.text: [Slow and flat] I do not want to get flooded; when I lose control, I disappear for days.
case-marcus.suggestion: Losing days is something we need to take seriously. We can begin with what helps you stay present and agree on when to pause. The aim is to understand a small part of your experience at a manageable pace, not push through a memory.

case-marcus.text: [Slow and flat] Feelings are the problem. When I feel them, I drink, shut down, or lose days.
case-marcus.suggestion: Those reactions tell us we need to be careful about how we work. We can start with what happens before you drink or shut down, without asking you to open everything. That helps us understand what support and pace you need before going further.

case-marcus.text: [Flat] Why notice the guard signals when I am on alert all the time?
case-marcus.suggestion: If you are on alert all the time, asking you to notice more can sound exhausting. We can look for when that alertness changes and what helps it ease. That gives us something specific to work with instead of asking you to monitor every signal.

case-marcus.text: [Hypervigilant] How will sitting with feelings help the nightmares instead of making the nights worse?
case-marcus.suggestion: You are worried the nights will get worse. We do not need to retell the nightmares to begin. We can explore how they affect you now and what helps you recover afterwards, then check whether any further work is helping or making things harder.

case-marcus.text: [Flat] How is working on connection supposed to help when being alone keeps people from wanting things from me?
case-marcus.suggestion: Being alone gives you relief from other people's demands. We can explore what kind of contact, if any, you would actually want. This is about finding support while keeping your choice and boundaries, not persuading you to let everyone in.

case-marcus.text: [Flat] What does progress look like for me if feeling normal is off the table?
case-marcus.suggestion: We can begin with what would make daily life more manageable for you. Progress might mean better sleep, a little interest in something, or an easier moment with another person. Looking for changes you value helps us decide whether the work is useful; "normal" does not have to be the measure.

case-marcus.text: [Low voice] Why should I trust this if therapists usually push for stories I do not want to tell?
case-marcus.suggestion: You have reason to ask how this will be different. I can explain why I ask a question and check whether you want to go there. That helps us choose the work together; you do not have to tell a story just because I ask.

case-marcus.text: [Hesitant] Can we keep this practical and not dig through every bad thing?
case-marcus.suggestion: Yes, we can focus on what affects your days now. Understanding the feelings involved can help us choose useful changes, without going through every painful event. You can decide with me what is relevant and what to leave aside.

case-marcus.text: [Slow and flat] What if I never feel normal again and this flatness is just who I am now?
case-marcus.suggestion: You are afraid the flatness is permanent. I cannot tell you now how it will change, but we can look at what makes life harder or a little easier. The aim is to find changes that matter to you, without requiring you to feel like someone else.

case-marcus.text: [Flat] Telling the story didn't help before. It just meant I didn't sleep. I'm not doing that again.
case-marcus.suggestion: You have reason to be cautious. We can begin with what happens here now, without retelling the events, and keep the work small enough that you can stay present and choose whether to continue.

case-marcus.text: [Guarded] The numbness lets me get through the day. Why would I want you to get rid of the thing that's keeping me going?
case-marcus.suggestion: We won't try to take your protection away. The aim is to find moments when you can feel a little without losing your footing, so numbness doesn't have to be your only way through the day.

case-arne.text: [Puzzled] Why talk about the empty cup? I know perfectly well she’s gone.
case-arne.suggestion: You know she’s gone. Noticing what the cup brings up might help us understand that lonely moment, if you want to try.

case-arne.text: [Curious] How would talking about guilt help me enjoy the workshop?
case-arne.suggestion: We could explore what enjoying it seems to say about your love for Eva, and see whether that meaning fits.

case-arne.text: [Unsure] Are we supposed to make me cry?
case-arne.suggestion: No. Tears aren’t the goal. We’re trying to understand what you feel and need, at a pace you can choose.

case-arne.text: [Questioning] Why stop when I mention feeling worn out?
case-arne.suggestion: That exhaustion matters too. Giving it a little room may help you hear it without turning it into proof you didn’t love her.

case-arne.text: [Careful] Do I have to talk about the day she died?
case-arne.suggestion: You don’t. We can begin with a present-day moment that you choose and see what feels useful.

case-arne.text: [Puzzled] What’s the point of asking what I notice in my chest?
case-arne.suggestion: Sometimes that helps find words for an unclear feeling. We can try briefly, or stay with words if that suits you better.

case-arne.text: [Concerned] Will sitting with sadness make the whole day worse?
case-arne.suggestion: It might feel stronger for a moment. We can take a small piece, check how it affects you, and pause rather than push through.

case-arne.text: [Curious] Why would we talk about the good afternoon as well?
case-arne.suggestion: That afternoon matters alongside the grief. We can hear what felt good and what happened when the guilt came.

case-arne.text: [Worried] Is this about learning to forget Eva?
case-arne.suggestion: No. We can work on living these days while making room for what she means to you.

case-arne.text: [Questioning] Why look at one evening instead of my whole life?
case-arne.suggestion: One evening gives us a manageable place to start. It may show what is hardest and what support you want then.

case-arne.text: [Unsure] Can this help with practical things, or just feelings?
case-arne.suggestion: Both can matter. Understanding the feelings may clarify a need; practical problems can also need practical help in their own right.

case-arne.text: [Careful] What if I don’t want to try an exercise?
case-arne.suggestion: Then we won’t do it. I can explain what it might offer, and we can choose another way to work together.

case-arne.text: [Skeptical] I’ve told this story before. What would be different here?
case-arne.suggestion: We could pause at one moment rather than retell everything, and check what it brings up now. You can decide whether that helps.

case-arne.text: [Careful] If I feel the relief properly, won’t that make me a worse husband?
case-arne.suggestion: Exploring relief doesn’t decide what kind of husband you were. It may help distinguish wanting rest from not loving Eva.

case-arne.text: [Questioning] You ask me to slow down. I’m afraid I’ll get stuck there.
case-arne.suggestion: We can slow briefly and keep checking your choice. The aim is understanding, not keeping you in a feeling you want to leave.

case-arne.text: [Unsure] Why pay attention to anger? I don’t want to blame her.
case-arne.suggestion: Anger may tell us about strain or an unmet need. Hearing it needn’t turn Eva into the problem; we can check what it actually means.

case-arne.text: [Doubtful] If we talk about a good day, are we avoiding the grief?
case-arne.suggestion: We can hear the good day and the grief together. What happens between enjoyment and guilt may be useful to understand.

case-arne.text: [Briskly] I need a plan for weekends, not more names for feelings.
case-arne.suggestion: A practical plan may be what you need. If useful, we can first clarify which parts feel lonely and what kind of company you want.

case-arne.text: [Hesitant] Will you make me say goodbye to her?
case-arne.suggestion: No. These exercises don’t require a goodbye. We can explore how you want to carry your connection with her into your days.

case-arne.text: [Puzzled] You notice my little laugh. Does everything mean something hidden?
case-arne.suggestion: Not everything. I noticed a change and want to check it with you, rather than decide what the laugh means.

case-arne.text: [Uncertain] Naming a need sounds easy. Asking Emma is another matter.
case-arne.suggestion: That’s a different step. Here we can find words that fit first, then decide whether or how you want to use them.

case-arne.text: [Concerned] What if talking about her makes the house worse tonight?
case-arne.suggestion: Let’s take that concern seriously. We can choose a smaller piece and leave time to consider the transition home, instead of opening more.

case-arne.text: [Careful] I’m not sure looking inside is my way of doing things.
case-arne.suggestion: We can begin with a concrete moment and your ordinary words. You needn’t adopt a new way of speaking to work with me.

case-arne.text: [Questioning] Why revisit a moment that already felt better?
case-arne.suggestion: Not to make it bigger. We could understand what shifted and what you want to keep, without promising it will stay that way.

case-arne.text: [Firmly] If the exercise ends with me forgiving everyone, I’m not doing it.
case-arne.suggestion: It doesn’t require forgiveness. We can explore what you feel and need; you decide whether the exercise is useful at all.

case-arne.text: [Watchful] You say feelings carry needs. What if mine are just messy?
case-arne.suggestion: They can be messy. This is a way to explore, not a rule that every feeling has one neat message.

case-arne.text: [Skeptical] Explain how this helps without promising me acceptance.
case-arne.suggestion: We might understand a difficult moment and find what would support you in it. I can’t promise acceptance, and it isn’t a required outcome.

case-arne.text: [Careful] I won’t do body scanning. It made me feel watched before.
case-arne.suggestion: We won’t use that. We can work with a concrete memory and ordinary words, checking what feels useful and comfortable.

case-arne.text: [Questioning] If I’m prompted to feel something, how do I know it’s mine?
case-arne.suggestion: That concern matters. Treat any prompt as an invitation, and tell me if nothing fits. We should follow your experience, not produce a feeling.

case-arne.text: [Dryly] I’m tired, not defended. Why keep asking about the feeling?
case-arne.suggestion: Tiredness may be reason enough to stop. Emotion work needs your willingness and energy; we can choose something less demanding today.

case-arne.text: [Firmly] I want a weekend plan before we explore another memory.
case-arne.suggestion: Let’s start there. Emotional exploration is optional; practical support can be useful without a deeper memory first.

case-arne.text: [Watchful] Is anger supposed to turn into sadness? I’d like my anger heard.
case-arne.suggestion: There’s no required sequence. We can understand the anger on its own terms rather than replace it with another feeling.

case-arne.text: [Skeptical] Don’t explain the method at me. Tell me what you’d like us to try.
case-arne.suggestion: A short pause at one moment you choose, then checking what you notice. We can stop if it offers nothing. Would that suit you?

case-arne.text: [Quietly] Talking changed something here last week. Home was still hard.
case-arne.suggestion: A useful moment here may not change home immediately. We can look at that gap and what support it needs, without calling last week a failure.

case-arne.text: [Careful] Don’t make a picture of Eva and tell me to talk to it.
case-arne.suggestion: I won’t. No imagined conversation is required. We can work in ways you choose, including simply talking with me.

case-arne.text: [Uncertain] I want to understand the guilt, not get persuaded out of loving her.
case-arne.suggestion: The aim isn’t persuasion. We can examine what guilt says about love and check it against your own experience.

case-mia.text: [Curious] Why talk about the pencil? It’s my hands that make me stop.
case-mia.suggestion: Talking won’t change that limit. We could explore what stopping means to you, if that would help.

case-mia.text: [Unsure] What would saying I’m angry actually do?
case-mia.suggestion: It might help us hear what you need respected. We can try briefly, without having to intensify it.

case-mia.text: [Questioning] Are we going to work on the tiredness or my feelings?
case-mia.suggestion: We can make room for both, and let your energy guide how much emotional work we do.

case-mia.text: [Hesitant] I already know that I miss drawing. What more is there?
case-mia.suggestion: We could find out which part you miss most. That may help us understand what matters to you now.

case-mia.text: [Practical] Could we work on asking Alex for help?
case-mia.suggestion: Yes. Exploring what feels difficult about asking may help us find words that fit you.

case-mia.text: [Wary] I don’t want to be made grateful for being ill.
case-mia.suggestion: That isn’t our aim. We can hear what this costs you without turning it into a lesson.

case-mia.text: [Curious] Why would we stay with that sad moment?
case-mia.suggestion: It may help you put words to the loss. You can choose how close we go, or leave it today.

case-mia.text: [Uncertain] Do I need to close my eyes to do this?
case-mia.suggestion: No. We can use your words with your eyes open; the point is to understand your experience together.

case-mia.text: [Tired] Is it worth starting when I don’t have much energy?
case-mia.suggestion: We could choose one small piece and stop when you need. Resting instead is also an option.

case-mia.text: [Curious] Would practising the words make Alex listen?
case-mia.suggestion: We can’t guarantee his response. Rehearsing may help you say more clearly what help you want.

case-mia.text: [Worried] Are you saying the pain comes from my feelings?
case-mia.suggestion: No. Your arthritis is medically treated. Here we can work with the feelings that accompany living with it.

case-mia.text: [Thoughtful] Why notice a moment that went well?
case-mia.suggestion: It may show us what helped you feel heard, so we can understand what you want more of.

case-mia.text: [Wary] If we explore the anger, won’t that make me harder to live with?
case-mia.suggestion: We could understand what it protects or asks for, without treating every angry reaction as helpful.

case-mia.text: [Practical] I need a chair at work, not insight about chairs.
case-mia.suggestion: Getting the chair matters. If useful, we can also explore what makes asking hard; insight won’t replace the adjustment.

case-mia.text: [Unsure] Part of me wants help. Part of me hates being helped. How does talking untangle that?
case-mia.suggestion: We could hear what each part wants in one real moment, rather than decide that one is wrong.

case-mia.text: [Tired] You say we can go slowly, but I’m worried I’ll disappoint you if we stop.
case-mia.suggestion: Stopping gives us information about the pace you need. The work isn’t to keep going for my sake.

case-mia.text: [Hesitant] If I let myself miss the old life, will I ever stop missing it?
case-mia.suggestion: We can’t promise that. Giving the loss words may make it less solitary, without requiring it to end.

case-mia.text: [Questioning] Would we practise asking Alex, or just analyse why I’m bad at it?
case-mia.suggestion: We can practise, while exploring what gets difficult. The aim is a request that fits you, not a judgment of you.

case-mia.text: [Wary] People keep telling me to accept things. Is this another version?
case-mia.suggestion: We can work with what is painful without deciding you should approve of it or stop seeking changes.

case-mia.text: [Quietly] I’m afraid that noticing a good moment will be used against the bad days.
case-mia.suggestion: We can explore what was good while keeping the bad days in view. One moment won’t become proof about your capacity.

case-mia.text: [Uncertain] Do we have to focus on my body? I spend enough time monitoring it.
case-mia.suggestion: No. We can follow words or a remembered moment instead. You choose whether attention to the body is useful.

case-mia.text: [Half-smiles] Is feeling less guilty going to make the laundry disappear?
case-mia.suggestion: No. We could explore guilt so you can decide about the laundry with less self-attack, alongside practical help.

case-mia.text: [Serious] I want to talk about my anger without you deciding Alex is the problem.
case-mia.suggestion: We can hear your anger and what happened, while leaving room for care and misunderstanding in the relationship.

case-mia.text: [Reflective] What’s the point of finding words if tomorrow I’m too tired to use them?
case-mia.suggestion: We can keep the words available without making them an obligation. What helps today may need adapting tomorrow.

case-mia.text: [Wary] If I can’t explain why I’m cross, will you just supply a reason?
case-mia.suggestion: We can explore without needing a finished explanation. Any guess of mine needs your correction, not your agreement.

case-mia.text: [Quietly] I can already describe the loss very well. I’m still living it.
case-mia.suggestion: Description may not be what you need today. We could explore one live moment, or choose practical support instead.

case-mia.text: [Skeptical] You say anger has a message. Sometimes I’m just cross and tired.
case-mia.suggestion: We don’t need to find a message in every reaction. We can check what fits this moment, including simply needing rest.

case-mia.text: [Firm] I’ll talk about asking for help. I won’t imagine my body doing things it can’t.
case-mia.suggestion: We can practise words for the help you want without imagining away a physical limit.

case-mia.text: [Uncertain] I’m not sure which feeling is the real one.
case-mia.suggestion: They don’t need to compete for that title. We could listen to each and see what you recognize.

case-mia.text: [Dryly] Are you hoping that if I ask nicely enough, people will stop dismissing me?
case-mia.suggestion: No. We can work on a request you stand behind, while recognizing that dismissal isn’t yours to fix alone.

case-mia.text: [Wary] I don’t want accepting help to become a test of whether I’ve progressed.
case-mia.suggestion: We can explore your choices without making a yes to help the required outcome. A no can fit too.

case-mia.text: [Thoughtful] What if sitting with the sadness only leaves me more tired?
case-mia.suggestion: We can keep it brief and check the effect together. We can stop or change direction if it costs too much.

case-mia.text: [Quietly] I want to understand Alex, but not explain myself out of being hurt.
case-mia.suggestion: We can hear the hurt first, and explore his possible intentions without letting them settle what you felt.

case-mia.text: [Questioning] Is remembering one good conversation supposed to change the whole picture?
case-mia.suggestion: No. It may help us identify what mattered in that conversation while keeping the rest of the picture intact.

case-mia.text: [Tired] If I say no to this exercise, will you keep offering until I say yes?
case-mia.suggestion: No. A no changes our plan. We can discuss another approach, or pause, without repeating the invitation.

case-mia.text: [Reflective] I want something I can use, not a beautiful sentence I’m too tired to say.
case-mia.suggestion: We can aim for a short request in your own words and check whether it is usable with the energy you have.
